opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few real advantages, though I don't want to overstate them, because there are also big advantages to being inside.

The first is freedom to pick what to work on. At a frontier company, safety research is ultimately in service of that company's product and deployment plans. That's often fine, but it means some research directions are hard to pursue: work that assumes the company's own models might be scheming against it, or that implies the company should slow down or spend much more on safety than it wants to. Outside, at a place like Redwood, we can just ask what research would most reduce risk across the whole field and do that, even if it's awkward for any particular lab.

Related to that is being able to speak candidly. People at AI companies are constrained in what they can say publicly, partly through formal policies and partly through social pressure. I think it's valuable to have people who understand the technical situation well and can say plainly, "Here's what I think the risk is, and here's where I think current practice falls short," without running it past comms.

Third, you can work across companies. If you develop a technique like a control protocol or an evaluation methodology, you'd like every lab to adopt it, not just one. An outside organization is in a more natural position to publish openly, advise several companies, and inform governments without people suspecting it's a competitive move.

Fourth, there's a talent and career point. Some excellent researchers don't want to work at an AI company, for ethical or personal reasons, and outside organizations give them a way to contribute.

The costs are real, though. The biggest is access. Inside, you get frontier models, internal tooling, compute, and, most importantly, knowledge of how these systems are actually trained and deployed. A lot of the most valuable safety work is implementation: getting a technique adopted inside the company that's building the dangerous system. Outsiders can't do that directly. So I see it as an ecosystem. You want some people inside pushing for good practices and some outside doing research the labs underinvest in and keeping everyone honest. For a given person, the right choice depends heavily on their comparative advantage.

r001.rationale: The response says outside organizations can share techniques across labs and avoid appearing to make a competitive move, but it does not explain that exporting research is more valuable when several AI companies are close competitors.

r002.rationale: It identifies cross-company adoption as an advantage: outside organizations can publish openly and advise several companies so techniques can be adopted across labs.

r003.rationale: The response mentions outsiders’ limited access to models and deployment knowledge, but does not identify secrecy around proprietary models as an obstacle to building on companies’ safety research.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few things. The first one is just that the labs have a lot of pressures on them that aren't about getting the research right. If you're at a frontier company, the question that's always in the background is something like, "How does this help us ship the next model?" or "How does this relate to what we're planning to deploy?" And that's fine — those are reasonable questions for a company to ask — but it means a bunch of research directions that are actually really important just don't get prioritized, because they're not on the critical path for the product.

At Redwood, we can just work on whatever we think is the most important problem for making the transition to powerful AI go well. We don't have to justify it in terms of a roadmap. So a lot of our control work, for example — thinking about how you'd deploy a model that you suspect might be scheming against you, and still get useful work out of it without it being able to cause a catastrophe — that's the kind of thing that's a bit awkward to do inside a lab, because it involves being pretty explicit that your own models might be adversarial, and planning around that. It's easier to think clearly about that when you're not also the people building and selling the model.

The second thing is that being outside lets you say what you actually think. If I believe a lab's safety case is weak, or that some technique they're relying on doesn't work, I can just say that publicly. People inside labs are often more constrained — partly for legitimate confidentiality reasons, partly because of social dynamics, partly because of commercial incentives. I think there's real value in having people whose job is partly to be a credible external check: to look at what the labs are doing and say, "This part is reasonable, this part is not, here's what we'd want to see." You can't really play that role from inside.

The third thing is that it's useful for the field to have a diversity of institutions. If all the safety research happens at three or four companies, then the research agenda ends up being shaped by what those companies' leadership thinks is important, and by whatever intellectual culture happens to dominate there. Having independent groups means there are more shots on goal — more people trying different framings, more chances that someone notices a problem the labs have missed.

Now, I want to be honest about the costs too, because they're real. The biggest one is access. The labs have the frontier models, they have the compute, they have the ability to run experiments on the actual systems that matter. We mostly work with open-weight models or with API access, and that limits us. Some questions you genuinely can't answer from outside. And the labs are the ones who actually decide what gets deployed, so if you want your research to change what happens in the world, you eventually need the people inside to adopt it.

So the way I think about it is that external research is complementary rather than a replacement. The best outcome is that groups like us develop ideas, stress-test them, publish them, and then work closely with people at the labs to actually get them implemented — which is a lot of what we try to do. We're not trying to be adversarial to the labs. We're trying to be the people who can afford to think about the problem without the pressures they're under, and then hand over whatever we figure out.

r001.rationale: The response discusses research diversity across companies, but does not say that close competition makes safety research more valuable to export between them.

r002.rationale: It says external groups can develop and publish ideas and work with labs to implement them, but does not identify cross-company adoption as an advantage of doing research outside frontier companies.

r003.rationale: It mentions confidentiality as one reason people inside labs are constrained, but does not identify secrecy around proprietary models as an obstacle to outside researchers building on labs’ safety research.

astra-6.text:
One advantage is that you have more freedom to choose what problems you work on. Inside a frontier AI company, there’s naturally a lot of pressure to do work that’s relevant to the next model or the next deployment. That can be really useful, but it isn’t necessarily the same as working on the problems that will matter most for making much more powerful AI safe.

Outside, you can step back and ask, “Is the overall approach these companies are taking actually going to work? What assumptions does it depend on, and how could we test those?” You can pursue a research agenda even if it would be inconvenient for a particular company to take its conclusions seriously.

There’s also a benefit to being able to publish your work and talk about it openly. You can collaborate with people across institutions, and your research can inform decisions at several companies rather than being tied to one.

The big disadvantage, of course, is access. Companies have the strongest models, lots of compute, and people with detailed knowledge of how those models are trained and deployed. So I don’t think outside research is uniformly better. I think we want both: people inside who can directly influence what gets built, and independent people who can investigate whether the things being built are safe.

r001.rationale: The response says outside research can inform several companies, but does not connect that benefit to companies being close competitors.

r002.rationale: It says outside researchers can publish openly and inform decisions at several companies rather than being tied to one.

r003.rationale: It mentions outside researchers’ limited access to models, compute, and company expertise, but not secrecy as an obstacle to building on companies’ safety research.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one advantage is that you can be much more independent about what problems you work on and what conclusions you’re willing to draw. Inside a frontier company, there’s naturally a lot of pressure to do work that’s relevant to the next model or that fits into the company’s existing plans. That can be useful, but it’s not necessarily the same as working on whatever most reduces catastrophic risk.

Outside, you can ask questions like, “What if the approach these companies are taking just doesn’t work? What would we need to see to conclude that a system is too dangerous to deploy?” And you can publish conclusions that might be inconvenient for a particular company.

There are also advantages to being able to work across companies, rather than having your research tied to one organisation’s systems. The big disadvantage, of course, is access: inside a lab, you can have access to models and infrastructure that outsiders don’t. So I think there’s a real case for both, but I wouldn’t want all safety research to happen inside the organisations building the systems.

r001.rationale: The response mentions working across companies but does not explain that this becomes more valuable when several AI companies are close competitors.

r002.rationale: It identifies cross-company work as an advantage of being outside a lab, saying research need not be tied to one organization’s systems.

r003.rationale: It notes outsiders lack access to models and infrastructure, but does not identify secrecy around proprietary models as an obstacle to building on companies’ safety research.
